The prototypes submitted for testing were to be single-zone packaged units with air -cooled direct expansion mechanical heating and cooling systems. The heating capacity for these systems were to be in the range of 10 to 25 tons, defined at an outdoor temperature of 5oF. This range was further divided into two categories, 10 to 14.9 tons and 15 to 25 tons, and prototypes submitted were to be recognized for meeting/exceeding the requirements in either category. Finally, the prototype submitted for testing was to be controlled using either of two external control methods. The first one specified using a thermostat while the second specified the use of a building management system in which the unit was to use normal communication protocols such as BACnet or Modbus. The latter required that a communication interface be provided by the manufacturer (e.g., an application to be operated on a separate laptop computer). 2.1.2 Cooling Performance The cooling performance was measured using the Integrated Ventilation, Economizing, and Cooling (IVEC) metric. The minimum requirements were as specified in Appendix A1 [1], which will become effective for equipment manufactured starting on January 1, 2029. For this CRADA, IVEC for the 10-ton prototype was to be greater than or equal to 13.4, while IVEC for the 15-ton prototype was to be greater than or equal to 13.1. Dehumidification performance was evaluated at the C test conditions with the unit operating at minimum capacity to demonstrate adequate dehumidification at low cooling loads. This was referred to as the DHC test. The unit could include dehumidification technologies such as hot gas reheat, desiccants, or others to provide adequate dehumidification at moderate outdoor air temperatures. Manufacturers were to show that systems can dehumidify at the 75°F outdoor air temperature condition specified for the IVEC metric in Appendix A1 [1] and account for cycling due to the low building loads at this outdoor air condition. Typically, the balance of sensible and latent heat capacity for an air conditioner is measured by the sensible heat ratio (SHR), which) is a figure that represents the ability of the system to dehumidify. It is defined as the sensible heat capacity divided by the total of the sensible and latent heat capacities. The measure of success in this test plan used this measure.
